Welcome!

1) It depends on the distro, just search "{distro I want to install} live USB". They'll all have instructions for creating one. Basically, it installs Linux to a USB drive, and you can boot to that and play around. If you enable persistance, it will even keep your settings and whatever you do in there. Note, when using a live USB, it will all be running off the USB, so it will most likely be slower than if it were installed proper. Just something to think about as you play around.

2) 2GB+ is generally fine. The drive can be reformatted afterwards.

3) Ubuntu, Linux Mint and Elementary are all good starters. Personally, I'd put them in that order.

Dual-booting is the same with all modern, user-friendly distros. When you go to install, it should ask you if you want to install alongside Windows.

How to do it: Individual distributions will have instructions for setting up a live-cd or live-usb configuration (this is what you'll use to boot into your distro' without actually installing). For most of the biggest/most-popular/most-friendly distros, this is as simple as just burning the image to a DVD/usb thumb drive and then booting up to that device. The new OS will boot and run from the installation media until you decide to install it. (both mint and elementary are this way)

For Mint (just as an example): Go here. It will walk you through the process of setting up a bootable USB drive. It's written for mint, but it will work for nearly any distro once you've downloaded the .iso file.

Size: Disk images (.iso files) for linux installs average around 1.2 to 1.5 Gb. Some are smaller. I haven't seen any that were significantly larger and certainly nothing in the 5+ Gb range.

Mint vs Elementary: Elementary is still pretty "young" (are they technically out of beta yet?), but last time I tried it things already looked pretty stable. Personally, I wasn't as comfortable with their UI decisions as I was with Mint so I didn't stick with it. But that's 100% a matter of opinion. Since you can download both Mint and Elementary (and every other distro) I feel like it's in your interests to try several versions and see what you like. Since you can use a reusable USB drive, you're not even wasting a blank DVD any more. So why not try them both and see what makes you happier?

Changing the look: Altering the look/feel of your installation is usually pretty straightforward. Right now, for example, I'm typing on an Ubuntu install. I like Ubuntu for its update schedule and easy of upgrading to the next version, but I vastly prefer Mint's Cinnamon desktop. So while I'm on an Ubuntu system, I'm using the Cinnamon desktop. Linux - as a general rule - is extremely customizable. That's sort of the point - you have access to everything down to the lowest bits of the OS, so you can do whatever you want to do with it.

Now that said, it's also pretty darn easy to find a pre-packaged version that has all of the major parts that you want out-of-the-box. While it was trivial to add cinnamon to Ubuntu, I know there's someone out there that has created a version of Ubuntu with cinnamon as the default.

Dual-booting is an excellent option, especially for a new user. It can be a little effort to initially setup (so read up on the details for whichever distribution you decide to install), but it gives you the "best of both worlds" while you're getting used to your new OS.

Privacy-wise, is dual-booting a secure thing to do, or will I need to put Windows on a separate device entirely? I'm considering editing all of my online information if it's insecure.

What you'll be doing when you setup a dual-boot environment is essentially created two different computers that share hardware, can see each other's hard disks and can only operate one-at-a-time. You'll have (you'll make) a separate partition on your hard drive (or on a second disk) that will house all of the linux OS materials, including your users' /home folders. The Windows partition will remain unchanged, but there will be a new/updated boot management utility that will let you pick which OS to use when you start the computer up.

While in one OS, you'll (normally) be able to see the other OS's disks, just as you might see a network share or external drive. So there are some potential privacy implications. I think your best bet will be to look at some folder/file-level encryption options. Both Windows and Linux (and OSX, fwiw) have multiple options out there and would ensure that someone in the other-OS can't read your personal files on this-OS.

I'm not 100% certain off the top of my head whether you could use full-disk encryption, or whether that would interfere with the boot-loader. You'll want to read-up on that if that's the direction you want to go.

Linux Mint and ElementaryOS are both derivatives of Ubuntu. There is very little difference in the core functionality of the two OSes, it's just that Mint, by default, looks far different than Elementary. However, this can be changed, usually with only one or two terminal commands.
